In short, it's checking to see if you have javascript enabled, and then it's asking you to perform some computations. These computations cost you a small amount of CPU power; a few seconds worth.

For a normal user, this doesn't add up to much, because a normal user doesn't send many requests. For a DDOS attack bot, which wants to send a massive number of requests, those few seconds would add up quickly, limiting the number of queries that it can submit that would get through to voat's actual server.

Yes it is to detect your likelihood of being a DDOS bot, by looking for traffic anomalies.

Its comparing the traffic the website normally gets to the traffic you are requesting. It looks at things like IP address, browser, OS, Geographic location, upload and download speed.

If you were plot all of these things on a bell curve to be able to see what the traffic looks like during normal operation of the site, you have a base point for which to compare. You could draw a bell curve of the distribution that is the normal users of the site for each of these attributes. Then if traffic gets large, you look for areas of the bell curve that rise much more than others. For example 80% of the DDOS bots might be running Internet Explorer, but only 10% of Voaters actually use Internet Explorer. So if the traffic request is coming from a browser that is identifying as IE, you can do math based on the percent of traffic increase to determine that for example anyone running IE is 90% chance of being a DDOS bot. Then you compare other traffic identifiers. Some may not be as useful for example operating system since most people use Windows. The OS may only for example identify a connection attempt as 50% chance of being a DDOS bot. The power comes when you combine all these odds together. Just combining the last 2 already lets us identify with up to 95% chance the connection attempt is from a DDOS bot. If you compare every single attribute of connection attempts to the history and trends of the website, you can eliminate a large portion of the DDOS traffic. For connection attempts that are suspicious, but not enough to block the website, traffic speed can be limited severely. Programmers can keep adding to this software to make it very complex and ever more accurate at detecting odds a connection attempt is from DDOS bot. For example a large company like cloudfare is able to leverage data across all of their clients and every IP ever to connect to any of their clients websites in the past have a reputation score based the odds they were a DDOS bot in history. Known and shared lists of suspicious IPs are also used to help identify the odds.

The goal is to give as high a percent of your traffic speed capability to the most legitimate looking traffic.
